```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaFin)
```

## The demo 3 FIN gap

`rolling_predict()` refits a lasso by ISTA on every rolling window of a
`T x p` panel. It uses `rcupp`'s **F0 one-shot operators**: each `rcupp_*`
call copies its operands host-to-device and back. That is fine for a single
fit, but a rolling forecast makes `n_iter * K` such calls, and the window
matrix `Xw` changes every step. The per-call fixed cost dominates, and the
original `benchmark/scenarios.R` recorded **demo 3 FIN 0/6** — the GPU path
lost to a pure-R fit in every configuration.

`rolling_resident()` resolves this with the **Phase-0 device-context C ABI**.
One `rcupp_ctx` uploads the full `X`/`y` panel once; each window is obtained
by a **device-side `gather_rows`** (no host-to-device traffic beyond `O(w)`
row indices), and each ISTA iteration calls `rcupp_d_prox_grad_step()` — on
CUDA a **single fused kernel launch** (both matvecs, residual scaling and the
prox in one block), replacing the ~8 per-iteration operator launches that
dominated the small `w * p` tiers. The solver loop stays downstream in this
package's C++; `rcupp` only supplies buffers and parts. `rcupp_ctx_abi()`
stays `1`, no new `rcupp` operator is added, and the code runs unchanged on
the CUDA backend and the CPU fallback (which composes the same level-1
operators with bit-identical numerics).

`strategy = "cold"` re-uploads each window from the host and is the ROI
baseline that isolates the transfer saving. Both strategies share the SAME
fused-step ISTA loop.

## Numerical contract

All four paths (`rolling_predict`, `rolling_resident` resident/cold, and the
pure-R reference) use the identical fixed-step ISTA contract, so their
coefficients agree to machine precision on both backends:

```{r parity}
set.seed(11)
n <- 60L
p <- 5L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
y <- drop(X %*% c(0.8, -0.5, 0, 0, 0.3)) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
w <- 30L
lambda <- 0.05
n_iter <- 120L

ista_ref <- function(Xw, yw, lambda, n_iter) {
  step <- 1 / sum(Xw^2)
  thresh <- lambda * nrow(Xw) * step
  beta <- rep(0, ncol(Xw))
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    r <- (yw - as.vector(Xw %*% beta)) * step
    u <- beta + as.vector(crossprod(Xw, r))
    beta <- sign(u) * pmax(abs(u) - thresh, 0)
  }
  beta
}
Xw <- X[seq_len(w), , drop = FALSE]
beta_ref <- ista_ref(Xw, y[seq_len(w)], lambda, n_iter)

f0   <- rolling_predict(X, y, w, lambda, n_iter)
res  <- rolling_resident(X, y, w, lambda, n_iter, strategy = "resident")
cold <- rolling_resident(X, y, w, lambda, n_iter, strategy = "cold")

data.frame(
  max_abs_diff = c(
    f0_vs_R       = max(abs(f0$coefficients[, 1] - beta_ref)),
    resident_vs_R = max(abs(res$coefficients[, 1] - beta_ref)),
    cold_vs_R     = max(abs(cold$coefficients[, 1] - beta_ref)),
    resident_vs_f0 = max(abs(res$coefficients - f0$coefficients)),
    resident_vs_cold = max(abs(res$coefficients - cold$coefficients))
  )
)
```

The `max |dcoef|` gate from the roadmap is `1e-12`; the measured value is
around `1e-16`. `make check` verifies this on both backends, and the CPU
fallback degrades gracefully (no device, identical numbers).

## Measured demo 3 result

The tables below are **snapshots** from a CUDA run (dense double `X`, single
GPU, `K = 60` rolling windows, `lambda = 0.1`, `T = w + K`), over the six
`(w, p)` configurations of `benchmark/scenarios.R`. `speedup` is
`t_r / t_resident` (pure-R over the GPU resident path); `ROI` is
`t_cold / t_resident`. Timing has a +/- 10-20% spread; read the trend, not the
exact decimals. Both sides always do the **same fixed number of ISTA steps**,
so this is an equal-work comparison.

### Short fit (`n_iter = 50`): the structural fix

Here `t_f0` is the old one-shot `rolling_predict()` path. It pays roughly the
same ~32 s in every configuration because the F0 per-call fixed cost
dominates, regardless of `w * p`. The resident path removes that cost, and
the fused ISTA step removes the remaining per-iteration launch overhead.

```{r short-table, echo = FALSE}
short <- data.frame(
  w    = c(500L, 1000L, 2000L, 500L, 1000L, 2000L),
  p    = c(40L, 40L, 40L, 120L, 120L, 120L),
  wp   = c(20000L, 40000L, 80000L, 60000L, 120000L, 240000L),
  t_r  = c(0.163, 0.200, 0.404, 0.263, 0.453, 0.991),
  t_f0 = c(36.167, 35.362, 33.970, 33.908, 32.566, 31.931),
  t_cold = c(0.125, 0.189, 0.333, 0.154, 0.269, 0.554),
  t_res  = c(0.099, 0.172, 0.313, 0.134, 0.249, 0.511),
  speedup = c(1.65, 1.16, 1.29, 1.96, 1.82, 1.94),
  roi     = c(1.26, 1.10, 1.06, 1.15, 1.08, 1.08)
)
short
```

The **F0 to resident** step is about a **200x** improvement
(`~33 s` to `~0.15 s`). Fusing the ISTA iteration into one launch also means
even at only 50 steps the pure-R BLAS path no longer wins: **6/6** configs
have `speedup > 1`. The sole remaining `t_f0`-based metric
(`speedup = t_r / t_f0`) stays `0/6` because the deliberately wasteful F0
one-shot path is ~200x slower — that is the baseline the resident path was
built to eliminate, not a target to beat.

### Realistic fit (`n_iter = 400`): the demo 3 gate

A real rolling-window lasso converges over hundreds of iterations
(`benchmark/scenarios.R` uses `max_iter = 800` FISTA). At `n_iter = 400`,
still equal work on both sides, the fixed per-call GPU overhead is amortized
over far more real work and the crossover moves down:

```{r real-table, echo = FALSE}
real <- data.frame(
  w    = c(500L, 1000L, 2000L, 500L, 1000L, 2000L),
  p    = c(40L, 40L, 40L, 120L, 120L, 120L),
  wp   = c(20000L, 40000L, 80000L, 60000L, 120000L, 240000L),
  t_r    = c(0.794, 1.647, 2.826, 2.092, 3.943, 9.886),
  t_cold = c(0.646, 1.147, 2.306, 0.863, 1.711, 5.153),
  t_res  = c(0.666, 1.139, 2.285, 0.854, 1.690, 5.168),
  speedup = c(1.19, 1.45, 1.24, 2.45, 2.33, 1.91),
  roi     = c(0.97, 1.01, 1.01, 1.01, 1.01, 1.00)
)
real
```

Now **all 6/6** configurations have `speedup > 1` (`1.19x` to `2.45x`),
including the three small/medium tiers that lost before the fused step
(`0.31x` / `0.61x` / `0.91x`). `max |dcoef|` is `2.44e-15`, well within the
`1e-12` gate. This exceeds the roadmap demo 3 target of `>= 3/6` — from
`0/6` originally, then `3/6` with the resident path, now `6/6` with the fused
ISTA step.

## Interpreting the numbers

- **Where the win comes from.** The dominant gain is F0 one-shot to resident
  operators (~90x): one `rcupp_ctx`, one `cuBLAS` handle, no per-call
  host-device copies. The device-side `gather_rows` (`resident` vs `cold`)
  adds a further, much smaller ~1.0-1.15x, because a single window re-upload
  is cheap relative to the many small kernel launches and the per-window
  scalar reductions (`dot`, `nrm2`) that still synchronize.
- **Why the small configs now win.** With the old 8-operator inner loop,
  `n_iter * 8` tiny kernels per window made launch overhead dominate when
  `w * p` was small, so pure-R BLAS won those tiers. The fused
  `rcupp_d_prox_grad_step()` folds a whole ISTA iteration into ONE kernel
  launch, removing that floor; even the shortest path now clears pure-R.
  The step adds **no new `rcupp` operator** and leaves `rcupp_ctx_abi()` at
  `1` — it simply makes the existing generic level-2 part live up to its
  "one launch per step" contract.
- **Honest scope.** This is fixed-iteration ISTA on dense double `X`, single
  GPU, and bounded `K = 60` windows. A single cold fit can still favor
  `glmnet` / pure-R BLAS (the F0 path here stays ~200x slower by design).
  The advantage is a repeated-fit workload: many windows, many solver steps,
  one resident panel. Timing has a +/- 10-20% spread; the largest tier
  (`2000 x 120`) dropped from `3.47x` to `1.91x` because the single-block
  fused kernel is now compute-bound there, but it remains a clear win.

See `?rolling_resident` and `?rolling_predict` for the full argument lists.
